newsitem.title: ITALY: FAO head welcomes U.S. involvement in Zaire mission.
newsitem.headline: FAO head welcomes U.S. involvement in Zaire mission.

text.p: The chief organiser of a United Nations food summit has welcomed U.S. involvement in an aid mission to Zaire while reminding ordinary Americans that they threw food away while millions were starving.

"I'm relieved and quite pleased that some concerted action is now contemplated," U.N. Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) director general Jacques Diouf told a news conference at the end of the opening day of the summit on Wednesday.
President Bill Clinton earlier tentatively agreed to order U.S. troops to join a humanitarian mission to help more than one million refugees facing starvation in eastern Zaire.
White House Press Secretary Mike McCurry said the U.S. commitment was expected to last about four months and involved dispatching 1,000 ground troops to the African nation.

While welcoming Washington's decision to intervene, Diouf said the situation in Zaire -- where more than one million people have fled fighting and face death by starvation or disease -- should never have been allowed to happen.
"We should not have to wait until people are dying...to have a Robin Hood policy," he declared.

Asked if there were three things he would like to tell "ordinary Americans" about the world food situation, Diouf drew attention to the division between the well-fed "haves" of the developed world and the "have-nots" elsewhere.
He painted a picture of Americans waking up, enjoying a hearty breakfast and driving to work on a full stomach.
"Then maybe they stop for a pizza or get two or three hamburgers during the day and then stop on the way home to get some slimming products," he said with a smile.
"They should know that there are 840 million people in the world who have no access to food...This is the first thing they should know, the second thing and the third."
Pope John Paul and U.N. secretary general Boutros Boutros-Ghali opened the five-day summit earlier with pleas for a global effort to resolve the Zaire crisis.
The Pope, who addressed the summit, later said that "no uncertainty, no excuse, no calculation" could justify any further delay in getting aid to the refugees.

The crisis was not on the official agenda but the immediate tragedy clearly weighed on the gathering, which opened with leaders adopting an ambitious plan to feed more than 400 million additional mouths by the year 2015.
Diouf said that by approving the declaration in advance, delegates could "for the first time in the history of United Nations summits" focus on actions rather than words.
Veteran Cuban leader Fidel Castro was earlier given a prominent role as one of six summit vice-chairmen despite being absent and was expected to have his say as well.
Diouf confirmed that the communist leader would be coming to Rome as planned but said he did not know when.

Security was more visible than at previous summit news conferences after three naked protestors disrupted a briefing by U.S. Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman to protest against genetic manipulation of soybeans.
